Software Architecture

The architecture of a software system  is a metaphor,
  analogous to the architecture of a building.

Software   architecture   refers  to  the  fundamental
  structures of a software system and the  discipline of
  creating such structures and systems

The architecture  of a software system  consists  of  it
  structures, the decomposition into components, and their
  interfaces and relationships.



                                                                                         Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                         2

--- PAGE 3 ---
The burden is on software

Hardware and compilers can keep up the pace needed.
From now on…
  ◦In shared memory programs:
     Start a single process and fork threads.
    Threads carry out tasks.
  ◦In distributed memory programs:
     Start multiple processes.
     Processes carry out tasks.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                         3

--- PAGE 4 ---
Parallel Programming Models

 1. Single Program Multiple Data (SPMD)
 A single executable program runs on multiple processors.
 Each processor executes the same program, but may follow
    different branches depending on data or processor ID.
2. Multiple Program Multiple Data (MPMD)

  Different processors execute different programs.
  Each program may operate on different datasets.

  Most Modern MPI based parallel programs follows SPMD model using MIMD
    architectures.
                                                                                                Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                         4

Writing Parallel Programs

1. Divide the work among the          double x[n], y[n];
      processes/threads
    (a) so each process/thread     …
      gets roughly the same             for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
     amount of work (load balancing)
    (b) and communication is                 x[i] += y[i];
      minimized.
2. Arrange for the processes/threads to synchronize.
3. Arrange for communication among processes/threads.

Multithreading

In computer architecture, multithreading is the ability of
  single CPU to provide multiple threads of execution
  concurrently, supported by the operating system.
Multithreading aims to increase utilization of a single
  core by using thread-level parallelism.
Multithreading allow for multiple request to be satisfied
  simultaneously, without having to service requests
  sequentially.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                         9

--- PAGE 10 ---
Shared Memory

Dynamic threads
  ◦Master thread waits for work, forks new threads, and when
    threads are done, they terminate.
   ◦Efficient use of resources, but thread creation and
    termination is time consuming.
Static threads
  ◦Pool of threads created and are allocated work, but do not
    terminate until cleanup.
  ◦Better performance, but potential waste of system
    resources.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        10

--- PAGE 11 ---
Process and Message Passing
Numerous  programming   languages  (message   passing
  paradigm) and  libraries have been developed for  explicit
  parallel programming.
The message passing programming paradigm is one of the
  oldest and most widely used approaches for programming
  parallel computers.
There are two key attributes that characterize the message-
  passing programming paradigm.
  ◦First, it assumes a partitioned address space (each process typically
    has its own private address space)
  ◦Second,   it  supports  explicit  communication  (Processes  must
     explicitly send messages to communicate with each other, and they
   must explicitly handle incoming messages).



                                                                                       Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        11

--- PAGE 12 ---
Partitioned Address Space

The logical view of a machine supporting the message-
  passing paradigm consists of p processes, each with its
  own address space.

Instances of such a view come naturally from clustered
  workstations  and  non-shared  address  space  multi-
  computers.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        12

--- PAGE 13 ---
Building Block: Send & Receive Operations

The interactions are accomplished by sending and
  receiving messages,
The prototype of these operations are defined as
  follows
 send(void*sendbuf, int nelems, int dest)
 receive(void*recvbuf, int nelems, int source)
The sendbuf points to a buffer that stores the data to be sent.
The recvbuf points to buffer that stores the data to be received.
The dest is the identifier of the process that receives the data.
The source is the identifier of the process that send the data



                                                                                         Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        13

--- PAGE 14 ---
Nondeterminism

     P0                   P1
      a = 100;                  Receive(&a,1,0)
      send(&a, 1,1);              Printf(“%d\n”,a);
      a=0;

• The important thing to note is that process P0 changes the value of a to 0
immediately following the send.

•The semantics of the send operation require that the value received by
process P1 must be 100 as opposed to 0.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        14

--- PAGE 15 ---
Structure of Message-Passing Programs

Message-passing programs are often written using the:
  ◦Asynchronous paradigm:  all the concurrent tasks execute
    asynchronously (no coordination) and
    make it possibly to implement any parallel algorithm.
    However, such programs can be harder to understand, and can have
      non deterministic behavior due to race conditions.
  ◦Loosely synchronous: In such programs, tasks or subsets of
    tasks synchronized to perform interactions.
    However,  between  these  interactions,  tasks  execute  completely
       asynchronously.
    Loosely synchronous programs  are  a good compromise between
      Asynchronous and Synchronous.




                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        15

--- PAGE 16 ---
Message Passing Types

Message passing is a method for processes to communicate by sending
  and receiving messages. It is how two processes (say Process A and
   Process B) exchange data via send and receive operations. It can be
   classified based on two factors i.e. blocking vs non-blocking, and buffered
   vs non-buffered.
1.  Blocking vs Non-blocking
   ◦Blocking: The process waits (is paused) until the operation completes.
   ◦Non-blocking: The process continues execution immediately after issuing the
      operation.
2.  Buffered vs Non-buffered
   ◦Buffered: Messages are stored temporarily in a queue or buffer until the receiver
      picks them up.
   ◦Non-buffered (Direct): The message must be delivered immediately — sender
     and receiver must synchronize.



                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        16

--- PAGE 17 ---
Blocking Buffered Message Passing

 Description:
    - Sender waits only if the buffer is full.
    - Receiver waits if the buffer is empty.
 If the buffer has space, the sender sends the message and continues.
    - The buffer acts as a temporary mailbox, so sender and receiver do not
  need to synchronize for every send/recieve.
 
   Process A (Sender)             Process B (Receiver)
    ------------------------                 --------------------------
   send(message) --->   [BUFFER] ---> receive()
              |
              | (waits if buffer full)
      V

     [message temporarily stored in buffer]



                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        17

--- PAGE 18 ---
Blocking Non-Buffered Message Passing

 Description:
   - No buffer exists.
   - Sender and receiver must both be ready.
   - The sender waits until the receiver has called receive(); this is
   called rendezvous communication.
 
  Process A (Sender)          Process B (Receiver)
   --------------------                  --------------------
  send(message) ---- waits ---->   receive(message)
        ^                              |
           |<----- synchronization ---->|

Both processes block until the message is transferred.



                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        18

--- PAGE 19 ---
Non-Blocking Buffered Message Passing

 Description:
    - Sender places the message in a buffer and continues immediately.
    - Receiver reads the message later.
    - Buffer must have enough space, otherwise message loss or error can
   occur.
 
   Process A (Sender)          Process B (Receiver)
    --------------------                 --------------------
   send(message) ---> [BUFFER] ---> receive()
         |                             ^
         | (does NOT wait)                        | (waits if empty)
       +----------------------------------------+
 
  The sender never blocks; receiver may block only if buffer is empty.




                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        19

--- PAGE 20 ---
Non-Blocking Non-Buffered Message
Passing
Description:
   - No buffer exists.
   - Sender sends and continues even if receiver isn’t ready.
   - If receiver isn’t ready, message is lost or an error occurs.

  Process A (Sender)              Process B (Receiver)
   --------------------                      --------------------
  send(message) ---> X (no buffer) receive()

  (Sender does NOT wait;
   message may be lost if receiver isn’t ready)





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        20

--- PAGE 22 ---
Blocking Message Passing Operations
A simple solution to the Nondeterministic behavior
  presented in the code fragment above is for the send
  operation to return only when it is semantically safe to
  do so.
It simply means that the sending operation blocks until
   it can guarantee that the semantics will not be violated
  on return irrespective of what happens in the program
  subsequently. There are two mechanism by which this
  can be achieved.
   1.  Blocking non-buffered send/receive
   2.  Blocking buffered send/receive




                                                                                      Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        22

--- PAGE 23 ---
Blocking non-buffered Send/Receive

In the  first case, the send operation does not return until the
  matching receive has been encountered at the receiving process.
When this happens, the message is sent and the send operation
   returns upon completion of the communication operation.
 Typically, this process involves a handshake between the sending
  and receiving processes.
The sending process sends a request to communicate to the
   receiving process.
 Since, there are no buffers used at either sending or receiving
   ends, this is also referred to as a non-buffered blocking operations.





                                                                                         Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS                        23

   idling at the sending and receiving process.
It  is also clear from the figures that a blocking non-
  buffered protocol is suitable when the send and receive
  are posted at roughly the same time.
However, in an asynchronous environment, this may be
  impossible to predict . This idling overhead is one of the

Blocking Buffered Send/Receive

A simple solution to the idling and deadlocking problem
  outlined above is to rely on buffers at the sending and
  receiving ends.

We start with a simple case in which the sender has a
  buffer pre-allocated for communication messages.

On encountering a send operations, the sender simply
  copies the data into the designated buffer and returns
  after the copy operation has been completed.

Blocking Buffered Send/Receive (1)

The  sender  process  can now  continue  with  the
  program knowing that any changes to the data will not
  impact program semantics.

Note that at the receiving end, the data cannot be
  stored directly at the target location since this would
  violate program semantics.

Instead, the data is copied into a buffer at the receiver
  as well.

Cache operation – overview

CPU requests contents of memory location

Check cache for this data
 If present, get from cache (fast)
 If not present, read required block from main
  memory to cache
Then deliver from cache to CPU
Cache includes tags to identify which block of
  main memory is in each cache slot



                                                                                                     5
Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 6 ---
Cache Addressing

Where does cache sit?
   ◦Between processor and virtual Memory Management Unit (MMU)
   ◦Between MMU and main memory

 Logical cache (virtual cache) stores data using virtual
   addresses
   ◦Processor accesses cache directly, not through physical cache
   ◦Cache access faster, before MMU address translation
   ◦Virtual addresses use same address space for different applications
     Must flush cache on each context switch

 Physical cache stores data using main memory physical
   addresses


                                                                                                     6
Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

7
Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 8 ---
Virtual Memory


Virtual memory is a facility that allows programs to address memory from a
   logical point of view, without regard to the amount of main memory physically
   available.


When  virtual memory  is used, the address  fields of machine instructions
   contain virtual addresses.


For reads to and writes from main memory, a hardware memory management
   unit (MMU) translates each virtual address into a physical address in main
  memory.


When virtual addresses are used, the system designer may choose to place the
   cache between the processor and the MMU or between the MMU and main
  memory.





                                                                       Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           8

--- PAGE 9 ---
Distributed Shared Memory

 Distributed  Shared Memory  (DSM)   is  a  form  of memory
   architecture  where   physically  separated  memories  can  be
   addressed as one logically shared addressed pace.


As the word “Distributed” is attached with the term “Shared” so it
   does not mean that there is a single centralized memory, but that
   the address space is “shared”.


 In DSM, data is accessed from a shared address space similar to
   the way that virtual memory is accessed.


 Information moves between main memory and secondary memory
   (with in a node) and between main recollections of various nodes.




                                                                                                     9Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 10 ---
DSM (1)
DSM  system  implements  the  share memory
  model  on  a  physically  distributed  memory
  system.

A shared virtual address space is maintained such
  that the same virtual address across processors
  refers to the same  logical  data, regardless of
  where that data is physically stored.

When implemented in the OS, such systems are
  transparent  to  the  developer;  whereas  the
  underlying  distributed memory  is  completely
  hidden from the users.



                                                                                                     10Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 11 ---
DSM(2)





                                                                                                     11Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

• DSM Implementation
   • Supported in both hardware and software.

• Hardware-Based DSM
   • On-Chip Memory
   • Bus-Based Multiprocessors
   • Ring-Based Multiprocessors

• Software-Based DSM
   • Implemented at the Operating System (OS) level
   • Implemented using libraries



                                                                       Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           12

--- PAGE 13 ---
On-Chip Memory

•  The CPU portion of the chip stores data.
•  The address  lines  are  directly connected  to  the CPU
  memory, enabling easy access.
•   It is expensive to implement.
•   Its construction is complex.





                                                                      Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           13

--- PAGE 14 ---
Bus-Based Multiprocessors
In  this  system,  a  multiprocessor  with  caches   is
  connected to the main memory via a shared bus.


Each processor has its own cache.


The cache helps reduce network traffic.


Prevention  algorithms   are   required   to   avoid
  simultaneous memory access by multiple CPUs.





                                                                       Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           14

--- PAGE 15 ---
Ring-Based Multiprocessors

 Ring-Based DSM does not have a global centralized memory.
 All nodes are connected via a token-passing ring.
 In Ring-Based DSM, a single address line is divided into a shared
   area.
 The single address space  is  split into a private and a shared
    section.
 The private section is further divided into regions, allowing each
   machine to maintain its own stack for unshared data.
 The shared section is accessible to all nodes.





                                                                                                    15Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 16 ---
OS-Implemented DSM

DSM system is implemented at the operating system level.

The DSM system is responsible for managing distributed memory across
    multiple nodes in the system.

To application developers,  the DSM system appears as a single, unified
   shared memory space.

 Developers can write their applications using standard shared memory
   programming paradigms and APIs without needing to explicitly manage
    distributed memory or communication between nodes.

The DSM system handles the underlying complexities of distributed
   memory management  transparently, abstracting them away from the
   developers.



                                                                                                     16Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 17 ---
Library or Language-Level Software DSM

DSM  system  is  implemented  as  a  library  or  language
   extension that developers can use in their applications.

 Unlike  OS-implemented  DSM,  software DSM  libraries
   provide  a  higher-level  interface  for managing  distributed
  memory.

 Developers need to use specific APIs or language constructs
   provided by the DSM library to explicitly manage distributed
  memory and coordinate access between nodes.

 Software DSM libraries often require developers to write
   their applications in a specific programming paradigm.



                                                                                                     17Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 18 ---
Software based DSM





                                                                                                     18Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 19 ---
Implementing DSM in software
There are three ways of implementing a software
  distributed share memory:

 1.  Page based approach  using  the  system  virtual
   memory;


    1. The DSM system intercepts memory access requests and dynamically

   manages the mapping  of  virtual memory pages to  physical memory

   locations distributed across multiple nodes.

    2. In this scenario, the DSM functionality is deeply integrated in to the

   operating   system’s  memory  management   infrastructure,  allowing

   processes to access shared memory transparently as if it were part of the

   system’s virtual memory.

                                                                                                     19Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 20 ---
Implementation DSM (1)

1.  Shared variable approach using some routines to access
    shared variables;

   1. DSM functionality is provided by external libraries that developers link with
   their applications.

   2. These  libraries manage  the  coordination and  synchronization  of shared
  memory access.


2. Object based approach ideally accessing shared data through
object oriented discipline.

   1. DSM libraries provide support for encapsulating shared data within objects.

   2. DSM  functionality   is  provided  by  libraries  that  offer  object-oriented
   abstractions for managing shared memory.


                                                                       Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           20

--- PAGE 21 ---
Advantages of DSM

 Scales well with a large number of nodes.
   ◦Unlimited number  of nodes  can be  used. Unlike  multiprocessor
      systems where main memory  is accessed  via a common bus, thus
       limiting the size of the multiprocessor system.


 Message passing is hidden –
   ◦Hide data movement and provide a simpler abstraction for sharing
       data.
   ◦Programmers don't need to worry about memory transfers between
     machines like when using the message passing model.


 Allows  the  passing  of complex  structures  by  reference,  simplifying
   algorithm development for distributed applications.


 Takes advantage of  "locality of reference" by moving the entire page
    containing the data referenced rather than just the piece of data.
                                                                                                     21Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 22 ---
Advantages of DSM (1)


Cheaper to build than multiprocessor systems.

Ideas can be implemented using normal hardware and do not require
   anything complex to connect the shared memory to the processors.

Larger memory sizes are available to programs, by combining all physical
  memory of all nodes. This large memory will not incur disk latency due
   to swapping like in traditional distributed systems.

Unlimited number of nodes can be used. Unlike multiprocessor systems
  where main memory is accessed via a common bus, thus limiting the size
   of the multiprocessor system.

Programs written for shared memory multiprocessors can be run on
  DSM systems,





                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS           22

--- PAGE 23 ---
Disadvantage of DSM

Few disadvantage of DSM are given below:

1.   Generally slower to access than non-distributed share memory.

2.   Must provide additional protection against simultaneous accesses to
     shared data.

3.   May incur a performance penalty.

4.    Little programmer control over actual messages being generated.

5.   Programmers need to understand consistency model, to write correct
    programs

6.  DSM implementation uses asynchronous message passing and hence
    cannot be more efficient than message passing implementations.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Message Passing Interface

Programming Using the Message Passing Paradigm
   ◦Oldest and most widely used approach for distributed
     programming.
  ◦The  logical view of a machine supporting the message
     passing paradigm consists of p processes, each with its own
     exclusive address space.
  ◦Most  of  the  communication   is  done  using  simple
     send/receive message passing.

 Characteristics
   ◦Provides high scalability
  ◦Complex to program
  ◦High communication costs



                                                                                                                       4Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 5 ---
Principles of Message-Passing Programming

Key Attributes:
   ◦Assumes partitioned address space.
   ◦Supports only explicit parallelization.
 Partitioned Address Space:
   ◦Each process has exclusive address space.
   ◦Data must be explicitly partitioned and placed.
   ◦Encourages locality of access.
   ◦Requires cooperation for interactions between processes.
 Explicit Two-Way Interactions:
   ◦Adds complexity but makes programmers aware of costs.
   ◦Encourages algorithms minimizing interactions.
    ◦Efficiently implemented on various architectures.
 Explicit Parallelization:
   ◦Programmer responsible for identifying parallelism.
   ◦Hard and intellectually demanding but can achieve high performance.

                                                                                                                       5Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 6 ---
Structure of Message-Passing Programs

 Programming Paradigms:
 Asynchronous:
   ◦Tasks execute independently.
   ◦Harder to reason about, prone to non-deterministic behavior.
 Loosely Synchronous:
   ◦Tasks synchronize for interactions.
    ◦Still easy to reason about, allows asynchronous execution.


 Single Program Multiple Data (SPMD) Approach:
   ◦Most common in message-passing programming.
   ◦Each process executes identical code.
   ◦Offers flexibility while maintaining scalability.
  ◦Can be loosely synchronous or completely asynchronous.




                                                                                                                       6Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 7 ---
Message Passing Interface (MPI)

MPI defines a standard library for message-passing that can be used to develop portable
   message passing programs.
The MPI standard defines both the syntax as well as the semantics of a core set of
   library routines.
 It is possible to write fully-functional message-passing programs by using only the six
   routines.





                                                                                                                  Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 8 ---
Identifying MPI processes

Common practice to identify processes by nonnegative
  integer ranks.

p processes are numbered 0, 1, 2, .. p-1





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 9 ---
Starting and Terminating the MPI Library
 MPI_Init is called prior to any calls to other MPI routines. Its
   purpose is to initialize the MPI environment.
 MPI_Finalize is called at the end of the computation, and it
   performs  various  clean-up  tasks  to  terminate  the MPI
   environment.
The prototypes of these two functions are:
    int MPI_Init(int*argc, char ***argv)
    int MPI_Finalize()
 MPI_Init  also  strips  off  any MPI  related  command-line
   arguments.
 •All MPI routines, data-types, and constants are prefixed by
   “MPI_”. The  return code  for  successful  completion  is
  MPI_SUCCESS.



                                                                                                                      9Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 10 ---
Communicators

A communicator defines a communication domain
  ◦a set of processes that can communicate with each other.
 Information  about  communication  domains   is
  stored in variables of type MPI_Comm.
Communicators  are  used  as  arguments  to   all
  message transfer MPI routines.
A process can belong to many different (possibly
  overlapping) communication domains.
MPI   defines   a   default  communicator   called
  MPI_COMM_WORLD  which  includes   all  the
  processes.




                                                                                                                     10Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 11 ---
Querying Information


The MPI_Comm_sizeand MPI_Comm_rankfunctions  are
   used to determine the number of processes and the label
   of the calling process, respectively.

The calling sequences of these routines are as follows:
       int MPI_Comm_size(MPI_Commcomm, int*size)
       int MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_Commcomm, int*rank)

The rank of a process is an integer that ranges from zero
  up to the size of the communicator minus one.

int
main (int argc, char **argv)
{
  int num_procs;
  int rank;

  MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
  MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &num_procs);
  MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);

  printf("%d: hello (p=%d)\n", rank, num_procs);
  round_robin(rank, num_procs);
  printf("%d: goodbye\n", rank);

  MPI_Finalize();
}

Issues with send and receive

  don’t make assumptions!

--- PAGE 39 ---
Deadlocks→Solution

We can break the circular wait to avoid deadlocks as follows:





                                                                                               Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 40 ---
Explanation

 This new implementation partitions the processes into two groups.
   ◦odd-numbered processes and
   ◦the even-numbered processes.


The odd-numbered processes perform a send followed by a receive,
 and the even-numbered processes perform a receive followed by a send.


 Thus, when an odd-numbered process calls MPI_Send, the target process (which has an
   even number) will call MPI_Recv to receive that message, before attempting to send its own
   message.





                                                                                        Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 41 ---
Avoiding deadlocks using Simultaneous
  sendReceive operation

To avoid earlier deadlocks, MPI provides MPI_Sendrecv function
  ◦It can both send and receive message
  ◦Does not suffers from the circular deadlock problems
  ◦One can think MPI_Sendrecv as allowing data to travel for both send and
    receive simultaneously.





                                                                                               Dr. Muhammad Asim, ICS/IT, FMCS

--- PAGE 42 ---
MPI_Sendrecv_replace function
  ◦If we wish to use the same buffer for both send and receive
  ◦First sends value[s] of current buffer and then overwrites them with
    received ones
Syntax

FILE 13/33: Mids Preparation\parallel.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 612 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 10000000

int main()
{
    static int array[ARRAY_SIZE];   // static allocation to avoid stack overflow
    long long sum = 0;              // long long to prevent overflow

    // Initialize array
    for (int i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE; i++)
    {
        array[i] = i + 1;
    }

    // Parallel for WITH reduction -> correct and deterministic
    #pragma omp parallel for //reduction(+:sum)
    for (int i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE; i++)
    {
        sum += array[i];
    }

    printf("Sum with reduction: %lld\n", sum);
    return 0;
}
